claims.claim: Pheromone recognition induces G2 cell cycle arrest and formation of long conjugation tubes in U. maydis.
claims.source: This recognition induces G2 cell cycle arrest as well as the formation of long conjugation tubes (García-Muse et al., 2003; Spellig et al., 1994), which grow toward each other and fuse at their tips (Snetselaar et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to García-Muse et al., 2003, Spellig et al., 1994, and Snetselaar et al., 1996.

claims.claim: Cytoplasmic fusion in U. maydis is not followed by karyogamy, resulting in a dikaryotic cell.
claims.source: Cytoplasmic fusion is not followed by karyogamy, resulting in a dikaryotic cell.
claims.evidence: This describes the unique cellular outcome of mating in U. maydis.

claims.claim: After cell fusion, the G2 cell cycle arrest is sustained during growth of the infective filament.
claims.source: After cell fusion on the plant surface, the G2 cell cycle arrest is sustained, and the single dikaryotic cell grows in a polar manner, producing the infective filament.
claims.evidence: This describes the continuation of cell cycle arrest after mating.

claims.claim: The infective filament grows by accumulating cytoplasm at the tip while distal parts become vacuolated and sealed off by septa.
claims.source: This hypha expands, accumulating the cytoplasm at the tip of the filament, whereas the distal parts of the hypha become vacuolated and are sealed off by the insertion of regularly spaced septa, resulting in the formation of characteristic empty sections (Steinberg et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Steinberg et al., 1998.

claims.claim: The hyphae eventually stop polar growth and form appressoria to penetrate the plant cuticle.
claims.source: Eventually, the hyphae stop polar growth in response to an as yet unidentified signal, and their tips swell to form appressoria and penetrate the cuticle (Snetselaar and Mims, 1992; Snetselaar and Mims, 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Snetselaar and Mims, 1992 and 1993.

claims.claim: Once the filament enters the plant, the cell cycle is reactivated and the fungus proliferates inside the plant.
claims.source: Once the filament enters the plant, the cell cycle is reactivated, and the fungus proliferates inside the plant.
claims.evidence: This describes the resumption of cell cycle progression after plant entry.

claims.claim: A sustained G2 cell cycle arrest is mandatory during differentiation for plant penetration, and its impairment results in inability to infect plants.
claims.source: During the differentiation process resulting in plant penetration, the presence of a sustained G2 cell cycle arrest is mandatory and the impairment of this cell cycle arrest resulted in the inability of the fungus to infect plants (Castanheira and Pérez-Martín, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Castanheira and Pérez-Martín, 2015.

claims.claim: Cell cycle arrest is first imposed by the pheromone cascade and then maintained by the b-factor during growth of the infective filament.
claims.source: This cell cycle arrest is imposed first by the activation of the pheromone cascade and then maintained during the growth of the infective filament by a transcriptional regulator called b-factor, which is encoded in the b-locus and composed of two subunits (bW and bE), provided by each mating partner.
claims.evidence: This describes the temporal sequence of cell cycle control mechanisms.

claims.claim: The b-factor arrests the cell cycle by activating the DNA damage response and repressing hsl1 transcription.
claims.source: The b-factor activates the DNA damage response (de Sena-Tomás et al., 2011; Mielnichuk et al., 2009) in the absence of DNA damage (Tenorio-Gómez et al., 2015), resulting in the phosphorylation of Cdc25, promoting thereby its interaction with 14-3-3 proteins, which in turn inactivates the phosphatase by its retention in the cytoplasm (Mielnichuk and Pérez-Martín, 2008); at the same time, the b-factor represses the transcription of hsl1, which encodes a kinase that downregulates Wee1 kinase, increasing as a consequence the level of inhibitory phosphorylation of Cdk1 (Castanheira et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing the mechanism of b-factor-induced cell cycle arrest.

claims.claim: The b-factor activates transcription of biz1, which represses clb1 transcription.
claims.source: Moreover, a second cell cycle brake is added during the formation of the infective filament since the b-factor also activates the transcription of biz1, a transcriptional regulator that represses the transcription of clb1, encoding the b cyclin required for the second Cdk1-cyclin complex involved in G2/M transition (Flor-Parra et al., 2006; Garcia-Muse, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Flor-Parra et al., 2006 and Garcia-Muse, 2004.

claims.claim: Expression of the fuz7DD allele faithfully recapitulates the pheromone response in U. maydis.
claims.source: Since changes in nutritional conditions could alter the cell cycle pattern in this fungus (Pérez-Martín et al., 2006), we took advantage of the previous description of an activated allele of the pheromone cascade MAPKK Fuz7 (fuz7DD, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), whose expression faithfully recapitulates the pheromone response in U. maydis (Müller et al., 2003; Zarnack et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Müller et al., 2003 and Zarnack et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Cells expressing the fuz7DD allele accumulate 2C DNA content.
claims.source: When an ectopic copy of the fuz7DD allele was expressed under the control of the crg1 promoter (induced by arabinose and repressed by glucose) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D), it mimicked the G2 cell cycle arrest observed when pheromone is sensed by U. maydis (García-Muse et al., 2003): cells accumulate 2C DNA content, carrying a single nucleus with an intact nuclear membrane (U. maydis breaks down its nuclear envelope at mitosis; Straube et al., 2005) (Figure 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 1A and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The fuz7DD-induced cell cycle arrest is dependent on Kpp2 but independent of Prf1.
claims.source: Furthermore, this cell cycle arrest was dependent on Kpp2, the downstream MAPK, but independent of Prf1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Cells expressing the fuz7DD allele show increased levels of Cdk1 inhibitory phosphorylation.
claims.source: We observed that the expression of the fuz7DD allele was correlated with an increase in the level of inhibitory phosphorylation of Cdk1, which has been reported to be associated with G2 cell cycle arrest in U. maydis (Sgarlata and Pérez-Martín, 2005a; Sgarlata and Pérez-Martín, 2005b) (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Impairment of Cdk1 inhibitory phosphorylation abrogates fuz7DD-dependent cell cycle arrest.
claims.source: Moreover, the impairment of Cdk1 inhibitory phosphorylation, either by the expression of cdk1AF, an allele refractory to inhibitory phosphorylation, or by the downregulated expression of wee1, the cognate kinase responsible for inhibitory phosphorylation (Sgarlata and Pérez-Martín, 2005b), abrogated the fuz7DD-dependent cell cycle arrest (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–F, and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The G2 cell cycle arrest associated with pheromone cascade activation is dependent on inhibitory phosphorylation of Cdk1.
claims.source: These results supported the notion that the G2 cell cycle arrest associated with the activation of the pheromone cascade was dependent on the inhibitory phosphorylation of Cdk1.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing that preventing Cdk1 phosphorylation prevents cell cycle arrest.

claims.claim: Expression of the fuz7DD allele strongly downregulates hsl1 transcription.
claims.source: Moreover, in agreement with a previous report (Zarnack et al., 2008), we observed that the transcription of hsl1, a negative regulator of the Wee1 kinase, was strongly downregulated upon expression of the fuz7DD allele (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), as it occurs in b-dependent cell cycle arrest (Castanheira et al., 2014; Heimel et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Chk1 is not involved in fuz7DD-dependent cell cycle arrest.
claims.source: However, our results indicated that Chk1 was not involved in fuz7DD-dependent cell cycle arrest (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: Expression of the fuz7DD allele does not upregulate biz1 expression.
claims.source: In the same way, it was already reported that expression of the fuz7DD allele does not upregulate biz1 expression (Flor-Parra et al., 2006; Zarnack et al., 2008), suggesting different mechanisms for pheromone- and b-dependent cell cycle arrest.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Flor-Parra et al., 2006 and Zarnack et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Protein levels of Cdc25 drop abruptly upon expression of the fuz7DD allele.
claims.source: We observed that the protein levels of Cdc25 dropped abruptly upon expression of the fuz7DD allele, although this decrease in Cdc25 levels cannot be attributed to a decrease in the mRNA levels of its gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 1E and qRT-PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: Overexpression of cdc25 does not abrogate fuz7DD-dependent cell cycle arrest.
claims.source: However, contrary to our expectations, overexpression of an ectopic copy of cdc25 does not abrogate cell cycle arrest, in spite of the presence of high protein levels of Cdc25 in these conditions (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: The decrease of Cdc25 levels is not the cause of pheromone cascade-induced cell cycle arrest.
claims.source: This result not only strongly suggested that the decrease of Cdc25 levels was not the cause of the cell cycle arrest, but it also supported our view of distinct molecular mechanisms between pheromone- and b-factor-induced cell cycle arrest
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that overexpressing Cdc25 doesn't prevent arrest.

claims.claim: High levels of Cdc25 can overwhelm b-dependent cell cycle arrest but not pheromone cascade-induced arrest.
claims.source: While high levels of Cdc25 do not affect the ability to arrest the cell cycle by the pheromone cascade activation, in the b-dependent cell cycle arrest, Cdc25 is retained at the cytoplasm by Bmh1 (14-3-3 protein), and this repression can be overwhelmed by high levels of Cdc25 (i. e. overexpressing Cdc25) (Mielnichuk et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This comparison is supported by a citation to Mielnichuk et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Pcl12 is required for induction of cell cycle arrest upon fuz7DD expression.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that Pcl12 was required for the induction of cell cycle arrest as well as for the observed decrease in Cdc25 levels upon the expression of the fuz7DD allele (Figure 2A and B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claims.claim: Crk1 is required for cell cycle arrest upon ectopic expression of pcl12.
claims.source: Furthermore, we also observed that Crk1 was also required for cell cycle arrest upon ectopic expression of pcl12 (Figure 2C and E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2C and E.

claims.claim: Crk1 and Pcl12 work together during pheromone cascade-induced cell cycle arrest, most likely as a complex.
claims.source: These results sustained the idea that Crk1 and Pcl12 were working together during the pheromone cascade-induced cell cycle arrest, most likely as a complex.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the genetic and biochemical data showing their interaction and mutual requirement.

claims.claim: Crk1 activation via phosphorylation by Fuz7 and Kpp2 is not required for fuz7DD-induced cell cycle arrest.
claims.source: Much to our surprise, we found that cells carrying crk1AEF or crk1AAA mutant alleles were able to arrest the cell cycle upon the expression of the fuz7DD allele (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Ectopic expression of pcl12 can arrest the cell cycle in cells carrying mutations affecting Crk1 phosphorylation by the MAPK cascade.
claims.source: Moreover, we also found that the ectopic expression of pcl12 was still able to arrest the cell cycle in cells carrying different mutations affecting the phosphorylation of Crk1 by the MAPK cascade, such as the loss-of-function in fuz7 or kpp2, or crk1 alleles refractory to phosphorylation (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Crk1 can be activated by two distinct mechanisms: as a MAPK by T-loop phosphorylation, or as a CDK by interaction with Pcl12 cyclin.
claims.source: We propose that Crk1, which is a kinase that have features of both CDK-like and MAPK-like kinases (see discussion section for a detailed description of this hypothesis), can be activated by two distinct manners: either as a MAPK, by T-loop phosphorylation through the pheromone MAPK cascade, to support polar growth; or as a CDK, by interaction with Pcl12 cyclin, to support cell cycle arrest.
claims.evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors to explain the dual functionality of Crk1.

claims.claim: Cell cycle arrest induced by ectopic expression of pcl12 is dependent on inhibitory phosphorylation of Cdk1.
claims.source: In support of this view, we observed that the cell cycle arrest induced by ectopic expression of pcl12 was dependent on the inhibitory phosphorylation of Cdk1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), similarly to the fuz7DD-induced cell cycle arrest.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Cdc25 levels do not decrease upon ectopic expression of pcl12.
claims.source: However, in clear contrast with the observed drop in Cdc25 levels upon fuz7DD expression, the levels of Cdc25 did not decrease upon the ectopic expression of pcl12 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: GFP-Cdc25 is excluded from the nucleus in filaments produced upon ectopic pcl12 expression.
claims.source: Strikingly, we also observed that in the filaments produced upon ectopic pcl12 expression, a GFP-Cdc25 fusion was excluded from the nucleus. Moreover, this exclusion was abrogated, as it was the cell cycle arrest, if the activity of Crk1 was eliminated (Figure 3A and B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claims.claim: The presence of Crk1-Pcl12 complex inhibits the interaction between Cdc25 and its importin Kap123.
claims.source: In support of our hypothesis, we observed that the presence of a Crk1-Pcl12 complex, but not G2 cell cycle arrest alone, disables the ability of Kap123 to interact with Cdc25 (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Upon fuz7DD expression, the mobility of Kap123 in SDS-acrylamide gels is reduced.
claims.source: We also observed that upon fuz7DD expression, the mobility of a Kap123-HA allele in SDS-acrylamide gels was reduced (Figure 3D), and this decrease in mobility can be eliminated by λ phosphatase treatment of the protein immunoprecipitates (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claims.claim: The decrease in electrophoretic mobility of Kap123 upon fuz7DD expression is sensitive to phosphatase treatment.
claims.source: We also observed that upon fuz7DD expression, the mobility of a Kap123-HA allele in SDS-acrylamide gels was reduced (Figure 3D), and this decrease in mobility can be eliminated by λ phosphatase treatment of the protein immunoprecipitates (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the phosphatase treatment experiment shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The decrease in electrophoretic mobility of Kap123 upon fuz7DD expression is dependent on Crk1, Pcl12, and Kpp2.
claims.source: The decrease in the electrophoretic mobility of Kap123 upon expression of fuz7DD was dependent on the presence of functional alleles of crk1, pcl12, and kpp2 (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Upon ectopic expression of pcl12, the decreased electrophoretic mobility of Kap123 is dependent on Crk1 but not on Kpp2 or Fuz7.
claims.source: In the case of ectopic expression of pcl12, Crk1 was required for the decreased electrophoretic mobility of Kap123, but neither fuz7 nor kpp2 were required (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: Kap123 belongs to the family of β importins of class 3 and 4.
claims.source: Sequence phylogeny analysis indicated that this protein (renamed Kap123) belongs to the family of β importins of class 3 and 4 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Kap123 is required for nuclear localization of Cdc25 in U. maydis.
claims.source: Therefore, we decided to analyze whether U. maydis Kap123 was required for the nuclear localization of Cdc25, and we found that it was (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C.

claims.claim: The Kap123T867A mutant allele shows no reduced electrophoretic mobility upon fuz7DD or pcl12 expression.
claims.source: The mutant allele Kap123T867A showed no reduced electrophoretic mobility upon fuz7DD expression and pcl12 expression (Figure 4B and C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claims.claim: Cells carrying the kap123T867A allele are unable to undergo cell cycle arrest in response to fuz7DD or pcl12 expression.
claims.source: Encouragingly, the presence of this mutant allele makes the cells unable to undergo cell cycle arrest in response to the expression of either fuz7DD or pcl12 (Figure 4D and E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claims.claim: Cells carrying the kap123T867A allele are unable to retain Cdc25 in the cytoplasm upon ectopic expression of pcl12.
claims.source: Moreover, cells carrying the kap123T867A allele were unable to retain Cdc25 in the cytoplasm upon ectopic expression of pcl12 (Figure 4F and G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claims.claim: The Kap123T867A-GFP allele is able to interact with Cdc25 in conditions of ectopic pcl12 expression.
claims.source: Also, we found that the Kap123T867A-GFP allele, in contrast to the wild-type GFP-tagged allele, was able to interact with Cdc25 in conditions of the ectopic expression of pcl12 (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: The pheromone cascade enables formation of a Crk1-Pcl12 complex that inhibits nuclear transport of Cdc25 by phosphorylating Kap123 importin.
claims.source: Taken together, these data supported a model in which the pheromone cascade enables the formation of a Crk1-Pcl12 complex that inhibits the transport of Cdc25 to the nucleus by the phosphorylation of Kap123 importin, thereby promoting G2 cell cycle arrest.
claims.evidence: This is a model synthesizing the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Cells carrying the kap123T867A allele are not able to arrest the cell cycle in response to synthetic pheromone.
claims.source: In concordance with our model, we found that cells carrying the kap123T867A allele were not able to arrest the cell cycle, even at the highest pheromone concentrations (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Pheromone treatment results in a shift in electrophoretic mobility of wild-type Kap123 but not kap123T867A.
claims.source: We analyzed, by Western blot, samples from these cultures and we observed a shift in the electrophoretic mobility of the wild-type allele but not the kap123T867A allele at different pheromone concentrations (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The kap123T867A allele prevents exclusion of Cdc25 from the nucleus in response to synthetic pheromone.
claims.source: Furthermore, the presence of the kap123T867A allele makes the cells unable to keep Cdc25 out of the nucleus in response to synthetic pheromone (Figure 5C and D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claims.claim: Strains carrying the kap123T867A allele are as virulent as wild-type strains in plant infections.
claims.source: We found that strains unable to undergo pre-mating cell cycle arrest were as virulent as wild-type strains (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by plant infection data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Crosses of kap123T867A mutant strains show a positive fuzzy phenotype, indicating ability to mate.
claims.source: We observed that although slightly impaired, the mutant crosses showed a positive fuzzy phenotype (i.e., they were able to mate) (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by mating assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Filaments from kap123T867A mutant crosses frequently carry two, three, or four nuclei.
claims.source: We found that the majority of b-dependent filaments from wild-type crosses carried two nuclei, whereas filaments obtained from mutant crosses frequently carried two (62% of filaments), three (35%) and less frequently four (3%) nuclei (Figure 6C and D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claims.claim: The kap123T867A allele does not affect the ability of b-factor to arrest the cell cycle.
claims.source: Indeed, we observed that the presence of the kap123T867A allele did not affect the ability of b-factor to arrest the cell cycle (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The lowest pheromone concentration tested (0.25 μg/ml) induces cell cycle arrested conjugation tubes but not Cdc25 downregulation.
claims.source: We found that the lowest pheromone concentration tested (0.25 μg/ml), although able to induce the formation of cell cycle arrested conjugation tubes (Figure 5A), did not induce a decrease in the levels of Cdc25.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Increasing pheromone concentration is correlated with a decrease in Cdc25 levels.
claims.source: However, increasing the amount of pheromone (up to 25 μg/ml) was correlated with a decrease in Cdc25 levels, suggesting a dose-response relationship between pheromone cascade signaling and Cdc25 levels.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: The downregulation of Cdc25 requires retention of Cdc25 in the cytoplasm.
claims.source: In support of this explanation we observed that the downregulation of Cdc25 levels requires the retention of Cdc25 in the cytoplasm, since expression of the fuz7DD allele in a kap123T867A mutant strain does not result in a decrease in Cdc25 levels (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Kpp2 is required for the decrease in Cdc25 levels upon fuz7DD expression under conditions of cell cycle arrest and cytoplasmic retention of Cdc25.
claims.source: In agreement with our hypothesis, we found that under conditions of cell cycle arrest and the retention of Cdc25 in the cytoplasm, Kpp2 was required for the decrease in Cdc25 levels upon fuz7DD expression (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Kpp2 interacts with Cdc25 upon activation of the pheromone cascade.
claims.source: Using GFP-trap beads, we were able to detect interactions between Kpp2 and Cdc25, which were dependent on the expression of the fuz7DD allele (i.e., high levels of MAPK signaling) and the presence of a wild-type Kap123 allele (i.e., retainment of Cdc25 in the cytoplasm) (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: U. maydis Cdc25 carries an unusually long N-terminal extension of approximately 270 amino acids.
claims.source: Compared to other fungal Cdc25-like phosphatases, U. maydis Cdc25 carries an unusually long N-terminal extension of approximately 270 amino acids with no similarity to orthologues in the database (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is a structural description based on sequence analysis.

claims.claim: Removal of the N-terminal extension of Cdc25 results in stabilization of Cdc25 upon fuz7DD expression.
claims.source: We found that the removal of this N-terminal extension resulted in the stabilization of Cdc25 upon expression of the fuz7DD allele (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: The cdc25AAA triple mutant is resistant to downregulation upon fuz7DD expression.
claims.source: Encouragingly, we found that the triple mutant was resistant to the downregulation observed in the wild-type allele upon expression of the fuz7DD allele (Figure 7G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 7G.

claims.claim: Neither deletion of the N-terminal extension nor alanine mutations in Cdc25 affect the ability of cells to undergo cell cycle arrest.
claims.source: Moreover, in accordance with our model explaining how the cell cycle is arrested in response to pheromone, neither the deletion of the N-terminal extension nor the alanine mutations affected the ability of cells undergo cell cycle arrest (Figure 7H) as well as the retention of Cdc25 at cytoplasm (Figure 7I).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 7H and I.

claims.claim: The MAPK Kpp2 targets and downregulates the phosphatase Cdc25, most likely promoting its degradation.
claims.source: In summary, these data strongly suggested that the MAPK Kpp2 targets and downregulates the phosphatase Cdc25, most likely promoting its degradation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing Kpp2-dependent Cdc25 downregulation and their physical interaction.

claims.claim: Sexually compatible strains carrying the cdc25AAA allele are strongly affected in their ability to produce disease in corn plants.
claims.source: Strikingly, we found that the presence of this mutant allele strongly affected the ability of fungal cells to produce disease to corn plants (Figure 8A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by plant infection data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: SG200-derived cells carrying the cdc25AAA allele are as virulent as the control strain.
claims.source: SG200-derived cells carrying the cdc25AAA allele were as virulent as the control strain (Figure 8A), suggesting a problem in mating associated with the presence of the cdc25AAA allele.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by plant infection data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: A cdc25AAA mutant cross shows a weak fuzzy phenotype compared to wild-type control.
claims.source: Moreover, a cdc25AAA mutant cross showed a weak fuzzy phenotype in charcoal plates, in comparison to wild-type control, indicating some kind of problem with the formation of the dikaryotic filament (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by mating assay data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: Cell fusion is not affected in cdc25AAA mutant crosses.
claims.source: We crossed mutant haploid cells carrying the dik6 reporter, and we were able to observe filaments carrying nuclear GFP signal, indicating that cell fusion was not affected.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the observation of b-factor-dependent GFP expression in crossed cells.

claims.claim: Filaments from cdc25AAA crosses are multinucleated.
claims.source: Interestingly, these filaments were multinucleated (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: A significant proportion of filaments from cdc25AAA crosses show more than five nuclei.
claims.source: In contrast to the multinucleated filaments found from crosses involving the Kap123T867A mutant, which seemed not to be able to bypass the G2 barrier imposed by the b-factor (we never found more than four nuclei per filament, Figure 6D), a significant proportion of the filaments observed in cdc25AAA crosses showed more than five nuclei (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: The cdc25AAA allele does not affect the ability of AB33 cells to undergo cell cycle arrest upon expression of compatible b proteins.
claims.source: However, we observed that the presence of the cdc25AAA allele did not affect the ability of AB33 cells (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1 for a description of this strain) to undergo cell cycle arrest upon the expression of compatible b proteins (Figure 8E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 8E.

claims.claim: During pheromone-dependent G2 cell cycle arrest, Cdc25 accumulates in the cytoplasm of conjugation tubes.
claims.source: We believe that during the pheromone-dependent G2 cell cycle arrest, Cdc25 is accumulating in the cytoplasm of conjugation tubes, but that as the compatible conjugation tubes are getting close (and therefore encountering higher pheromone concentrations) the subsequent increase in the pheromone-cascade signaling, promotes a decrease in the Cdc25 levels that allows a proper b-dependent cell cycle arrest in the filament once the cells were fused.
claims.evidence: This is a model proposed to explain the functional importance of Cdc25 downregulation.

claims.claim: G2/M transition in U. maydis is regulated by two distinct CDK complexes: Cdk1-Clb1 and Cdk1-Clb2.
claims.source: G2/M transition in U. maydis is regulated by the presence of two distinct cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) complexes: Cdk1-Clb1 and Cdk1-Clb2 (Garcia-Muse, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Garcia-Muse, 2004.

claims.claim: The limiting step for G2/M transition is provided by the activity of the Cdk1-Clb2 complex.
claims.source: Of these, the limiting step is provided by the activity of the Cdk1-Clb2 complex, which is controlled by the inhibitory phosphorylation of Cdk1.
claims.evidence: This describes the regulatory hierarchy of CDK complexes in U. maydis.

claims.claim: The level of Cdk1 inhibitory phosphorylation depends on the relative activity of Wee1 kinase and Cdc25 phosphatase.
claims.source: The level of this phosphorylation depends on the relative activity of the Wee1 kinase (which inhibits Cdk1) and the Cdc25 phosphatase (which activates Cdk1) (Sgarlata and Pérez-Martín, 2005a; Sgarlata and Pérez-Martín, 2005b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Sgarlata and Pérez-Martín, 2005a and 2005b.

claims.claim: Pcl12 forms a complex with the essential cyclin-dependent kinase Cdk5.
claims.source: Pcl12 forms a complex with the essential cyclin-dependent kinase Cdk5 (Castillo-Lluva et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Castillo-Lluva et al., 2007.

claims.claim: The Pcl12-Cdk5 complex is required for sustained polar growth during formation of conjugation tubes.
claims.source: The Pcl12-Cdk5 complex is required for sustained polar growth during the formation of the conjugation tubes in response to pheromone treatment (Flor-Parra et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Flor-Parra et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Cdk5 is not required for fuz7DD-induced cell cycle arrest.
claims.source: However, we found that Cdk5 was not required for fuz7DD-induced cell cycle arrest (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Crk1 was identified among the major peptides copurifying with Pcl12 in LC/MS analysis.
claims.source: We found the kinase Crk1 among the major peptides copurifying with Pcl12 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by proteomic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Crk1 was previously described as a regulator of polar growth whose overexpression induces cell filamentation.
claims.source: Crk1 (Cdk-Related Kinase 1) was previously described as a regulator of polar growth since its overexpression induces cell filamentation (Garrido and Pérez-Martín, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Garrido and Pérez-Martín, 2003.

claims.claim: Crk1 activation is linked to the pheromone cascade through phosphorylation by Fuz7 and Kpp2.
claims.source: Interestingly, Crk1 activation was previously described to be linked to the pheromone cascade: In order to promote hyperpolarized growth, Crk1 must be activated via phosphorylation of its T-loop by the MAPKK Fuz7, as well as by phosphorylation of the C-terminal end by the MAPK Kpp2 (Garrido et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Garrido et al., 2004.

claims.claim: The gene pcl12 is strongly induced by the pheromone MAPK.
claims.source: In our search for elements connected to the pheromone cascade that could be involved in the induction of the cell cycle arrest, we recalled the gene pcl12, which has been reported to be strongly induced by the pheromone MAPK (Flor-Parra et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Flor-Parra et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Ectopic expression of pcl12 is sufficient to induce formation of a cell structure resembling a conjugation tube arrested at G2 phase.
claims.source: This gene encodes a cyclin from the Pcl family (Measday et al., 1997), and its ectopic expression under a regulatable promoter (such as the crg1 promoter) was sufficient to induce the formation of a cell structure resembling a conjugation tube, which was also arrested at G2 phase (Flor-Parra et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Measday et al., 1997 and Flor-Parra et al., 2007.

claims.claim: U. maydis breaks down its nuclear envelope at mitosis.
claims.source: cells accumulate 2C DNA content, carrying a single nucleus with an intact nuclear membrane (U. maydis breaks down its nuclear envelope at mitosis; Straube et al., 2005)
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Straube et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Sal3 from S. pombe is involved in nuclear import of Cdc25 in this fungus.
claims.source: A previous report showed that Sal3 from S. pombe, which is one of the members of the class 3 β importin family, was involved in the nuclear import of Cdc25 in this fungus (Chua et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chua et al., 2002.

claims.claim: The importance of cell cycle synchronization before cell fusion during mating was illustrated by defects in S. cerevisiae far1 mutants.
claims.source: The importance of cell cycle synchronization as a step prior to cell fusion during mating in unicellular eukaryotes was clearly illustrated more than 25 years ago by the defects in mating observed in the S. cerevisiae far1 mutants, which lack the main control to arrest the cell cycle upon pheromone response (Chang and Herskowitz, 1990; Pope et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Chang and Herskowitz, 1990 and Pope et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Smut fungi are a widespread group of plant pathogens whose sexual development is coupled with virulence.
claims.source: Smut fungi are a widespread group of plant pathogens whose sexual development is coupled with virulence.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about smut fungi.

claims.claim: All smut species investigated have in common the need to undergo successful mating to form an infective dikaryotic filament before infecting their host plant.
claims.source: All smut species investigated so far have in common the need to undergo a successful mating reaction to form an infective dikaryotic filament before being able to infect their host plant (Bakkeren et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bakkeren et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Cell cycle arrest of the infective filament on plant surface is also present in rust fungi like Uromyces phaseoli.
claims.source: The cell cycle arrest of the infective filament on plant surface observed in U. maydis seems to be more general, and it is also present in rust fungi like Uromyces phaseoli (Heath and Heath, 1978).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heath and Heath, 1978.

claims.claim: In Magnaporthe oryzae and Colletotrichum orbiculare, infection depends on formation of appressorium.
claims.source: The connections between cell cycle regulation and the virulence in plant fungal pathogens have been studied in detail in other systems, in addition to U. maydis, such as Magnaporthe oryzae and Colletotrichum orbiculare. In these systems, the infection depends on the formation of appressorium, a structure required for plant penetration.
claims.evidence: This describes the infection mechanism in these fungi.

claims.claim: Appressoria from M. oryzae and C. orbiculare use a turgor-driven mechanical process to breach the plant cuticle.
claims.source: The appressoria from these fungi use a turgor-driven mechanical process to breach the plant cuticle.
claims.evidence: This describes the mechanism of plant penetration by these fungi.

claims.claim: There is a G1/S control to induce appressorium formation in C. orbiculare and M. oryzae.
claims.source: There is a G1/S control to induce the formation of appressorium, first described in C. orbiculare (Fukada and Kubo, 2015), but also operating in M. oryzae (Fukada et al., 2019)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Fukada and Kubo, 2015 and Fukada et al., 2019.

claims.claim: There is an S-phase checkpoint required for appressorium differentiation in M. oryzae.
claims.source: and there is a S-phase checkpoint required for appressorium differentiation in M. oryzae (Osés-Ruiz et al., 2017; Osés-Ruiz and Talbot, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Osés-Ruiz et al., 2017 and Osés-Ruiz and Talbot, 2017.

claims.claim: Appressoria of U. maydis are not dependent on turgor pressure to penetrate plant tissue.
claims.source: In contrast to appressoria from these phytopathogenic fungi, appressoria of U. maydis is not dependent on turgor pressure to penetrate the plant tissue.
claims.evidence: This describes a key difference in infection mechanism.

claims.claim: U. maydis appressorium directs localized secretion of enzymes that weaken the plant cuticle.
claims.source: The appressorium directs the localized secretion of enzymes that weakens the plant cuticle, allowing the plant tissue penetration.
claims.evidence: This describes the mechanism of plant penetration by U. maydis.

claims.claim: G2 cell cycle arrest is mandatory to promote differentiation of the appressorium in U. maydis.
claims.source: G2 cell cycle arrest is mandatory to promote the differentiation of the appressorium, and the impairment in cell cycle arrest resulted in a lack of virulence (Castanheira et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Castanheira et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Mitosis and the morphogenetic program for appressorium formation compete for the same cytoskeletal components.
claims.source: This obligation for cell cycle arrest at G2 phase is most likely related to the fact that mitosis and the morphogenetic program responsible for appressorium formation compete for the same cytoskeletal components.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation proposed by the authors.

claims.claim: Cellular controls exist to prevent infective filaments from entering mitosis due to competition between mitosis and morphogenesis for cytoskeletal components.
claims.source: Because of this competition, it makes sense that cellular controls exist to force these two processes to be incompatible and therefore to prevent infective filaments from entering mitosis (i.e., to arrest the progression of the cell cycle at G2) (Pérez-Martín et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pérez-Martín et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Both pheromone and b-factor regulatory networks rely on increasing Cdk1 inhibitory phosphorylation to arrest the cell cycle.
claims.source: The G2/M transition in U. maydis is controlled by the level of inhibitory phosphorylation of the Cdk1-Clb2 complex, and both regulatory networks rely on an increase in Cdk1 inhibitory phosphorylation to arrest the cell cycle.
claims.evidence: This describes a shared mechanism between the two regulatory networks.

claims.claim: Both pheromone and b-factor regulatory networks upregulate Wee1 kinase by transcriptional repression of hsl1.
claims.source: To achieve this increase, both regulatory networks upregulate the kinase responsible for this inhibitory phosphorylation, the Wee1 kinase. This upregulation is indirect and is mediated by the transcriptional repression of hsl1, which encodes a kinase that represses Wee1 activity.
claims.evidence: This describes another shared mechanism between the two regulatory networks.

claims.claim: Loss-of-function mutants in Hsl1 can progress through the cell cycle, although with an extended G2 phase.
claims.source: However, the repression of hsl1 is not enough to arrest the cell cycle at G2: loss-of-function mutants in Hsl1 are able to progress through the cell cycle, although they have an extended G2 phase (Castanheira et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Castanheira et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The pheromone cascade promotes formation of a Crk1-Pcl12 complex that phosphorylates and inhibits β-importin Kap123.
claims.source: The pheromone cascade promotes the formation of a kinase-cyclin complex, Crk1-Pcl12, which phosphorylates and inhibits the β-importin Kap123, which is required for the nuclear translocation of Cdc25.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claims.claim: The b-factor activates the DDR cascade resulting in Cdc25 phosphorylation and cytoplasmic retention via 14-3-3 proteins.
claims.source: The b-factor, however, activates the cascade responsible for the DNA damage response (DDR, composed of Atr1 and Chk1 kinases), resulting in phosphorylation of Cdc25, which promotes its cytoplasmic retention via 14-3-3 proteins (de Sena-Tomás et al., 2011; Mielnichuk and Pérez-Martín, 2008; Mielnichuk et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The b-factor also induces transcriptional repression of clb1 via the intermediate regulator Biz1.
claims.source: This downregulation of Cdc25 also provides a time window to load a third element (not present in pheromone-induced cell cycle arrest) consisting of the transcriptional repression (via an intermediate regulator called Biz1) of clb1, which encodes a second b-type cyclin that is also required for G2/M transition (Flor-Parra et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Flor-Parra et al., 2006.

claims.claim: The pheromone-dependent cell cycle arrest should be reversible if the stimulus disappears and mating is not successful.
claims.source: If for some reason this step does not occur, the unmated cells must be able to return to the previous vegetative status. In other words, the pheromone cell cycle arrest should be reversible if the stimulus (pheromone) disappears and mating was not successful.
claims.evidence: This is a functional interpretation of the biological requirement.

claims.claim: A control mediated by phosphorylation of importin could be easily reversed by phosphatase once pheromone signaling is abrogated.
claims.source: A control mediated by the phosphorylation of importin could probably be easily reversed by some phosphatase (specific or not) once the signaling through the pheromone cascade is abrogated.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation about reversibility.

claims.claim: The formation of the dikaryotic filament is a more terminal decision once mating partners fuse their cytoplasms.
claims.source: The formation of the dikaryotic filament, however, is a more terminal decision in the sense that once the mating partners fuse their respective cytoplasms, if they are compatible at the b-locus, the infective filament is committed to infecting the plant.
claims.evidence: This is a functional interpretation of the biological commitment.

claims.claim: Two independent cell cycle brakes make the b-dependent cell cycle arrest less reversible.
claims.source: The presence of two independent cell cycle brakes, provided by the retention of Cdc25 at cytoplasm by 14-3-3 proteins and by the transcriptional repression of clb1 could make this step less reversible.
claims.evidence: This is a functional interpretation of having multiple mechanisms.

claims.claim: Inhibition of nuclear translocation of Cdc25 cannot be bypassed by high concentrations of Cdc25.
claims.source: Although the downregulation of Cdc25 activity consists of the retention of Cdc25 in the cytoplasm in both regulatory networks, there is one relevant difference: while the inhibition of nuclear translocation (pheromone-dependent) cannot be bypassed by high concentrations of Cdc25, the retention of Cdc25 by 14-3-3 (b-dependent) is sensitive to the amount of Cdc25 (probably because of saturation of the available retention proteins).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the overexpression experiments.

claims.claim: Retention of Cdc25 by 14-3-3 proteins is sensitive to the amount of Cdc25.
claims.source: while the inhibition of nuclear translocation (pheromone-dependent) cannot be bypassed by high concentrations of Cdc25, the retention of Cdc25 by 14-3-3 (b-dependent) is sensitive to the amount of Cdc25 (probably because of saturation of the available retention proteins).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the ability to overwhelm b-dependent arrest with Cdc25 overexpression.

claims.claim: Crk1 belongs to the family of RD kinases with a conserved arginine-aspartate motif in the catalytic loop.
claims.source: Crk1 belongs to the family of RD kinases, which have a conserved arginine residue preceding an aspartate residue in the catalytic loop (Johnson et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Johnson et al., 1996.

claims.claim: RD kinases require an activation segment (T-loop) that undergoes conformational change to fold into an active catalytic site.
claims.source: For this reason, the members of this family require an activation segment (T-loop) that undergoes a conformational change to fold into an active catalytic site.
claims.evidence: This describes a general property of RD kinases.

claims.claim: The conformational change in RD kinases can be achieved by phosphorylation or by interaction with other proteins.
claims.source: This conformational change can be achieved either by the phosphorylation of specific residues (such as TxY in MAP kinases) or by interaction with other proteins (such as cyclins in cyclin-dependent kinases) (Nolen et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nolen et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Crk1 carries a TEY signature at its T-loop, similar to a MAP kinase.
claims.source: Crk1 carries a TEY signature at its T-loop, similar to a MAP kinase, but it is worth mentioning that it was cloned from a genetic screening devoted to uncovering CDK-like proteins in U. maydis and that the predicted three-dimensional folding of the catalytic domain of Crk1 fits the structure of Cdk2 (Garrido and Pérez-Martín, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Garrido and Pérez-Martín, 2003.

claims.claim: Crk1 belongs to a widely conserved family of fungal kinases, with Ime2 as the founding member.
claims.source: The importance of this alternative activation mechanism can be appreciated by considering that Crk1 belongs to a widely conserved family of fungal kinases, the founding member of which is Ime2, a central regulator of meiosis in S. cerevisiae.
claims.evidence: This describes the evolutionary context of Crk1.

claims.claim: Ime2-related kinases exhibit variety in controlling sexual developmental programs in fungi with species-specific targets and inputs.
claims.source: The Ime2-related kinases exhibit amazing variety in controlling sexual developmental programs in fungi, although the targets and physiological inputs seem to be very species-specific (Irniger, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Irniger, 2011.

results.result: U. maydis undergoes a unique G2 cell cycle arrest during mating and infection. Unlike most fungi that arrest at G1, U. maydis arrests at G2 phase in response to pheromone recognition. This arrest is initiated upon pheromone recognition in each mating partner and sustained after cell fusion until plant entry. The sustained G2 arrest is mandatory for infection, as its impairment results in inability to infect plants.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C13, C16-C26 collectively establish the biological context and uniqueness of U. maydis cell cycle regulation during mating and infection. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations to prior work (C7-C13, C16, C18-C19, C22-C23, C25) and describe established knowledge about the U. maydis system. The claims are internally consistent and provide the necessary background for understanding the experimental work.

results.result: Expression of the activated fuz7DD allele faithfully recapitulates pheromone-induced G2 cell cycle arrest. Cells expressing fuz7DD accumulate 2C DNA content with intact nuclear membranes, show increased Cdk1 inhibitory phosphorylation, and this arrest is dependent on Kpp2 but independent of Prf1. Preventing Cdk1 inhibitory phosphorylation abrogates the arrest.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C34 are supported by experimental data (FACS analysis in Figure 1A, microscopy in Figure 1B, Western blots in Figures 1C-D) and prior citations validating the fuz7DD system. The genetic dependencies (Kpp2, Prf1) are demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E. The conclusion that G2 arrest depends on Cdk1 inhibitory phosphorylation is well-supported by the cdk1AF and wee1 downregulation experiments.

results.result: Pheromone cascade-induced cell cycle arrest differs mechanistically from b-factor-induced arrest. While both downregulate hsl1, the pheromone cascade does not involve Chk1 or upregulate biz1. Cdc25 protein levels drop upon fuz7DD expression, but overexpression of Cdc25 does not abrogate arrest, indicating the decrease is not causal. This contrasts with b-dependent arrest, which can be overwhelmed by high Cdc25 levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C41 are supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), genetic analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), Western blots (Figure 1E), and overexpression experiments (Figures 1F, 1—figure supplement 4). The comparison to b-dependent arrest is supported by citation C41. The logic is sound: if Cdc25 decrease were causal, overexpression should rescue, but it doesn't, indicating a different mechanism.

results.result: Pcl12 and Crk1 form a complex required for pheromone cascade-induced cell cycle arrest. Pcl12 is a cyclin strongly induced by the pheromone MAPK, and its ectopic expression induces G2-arrested conjugation tubes. Crk1 was identified as a major Pcl12-interacting protein by LC/MS. Both are required for fuz7DD-induced cell cycle arrest and Cdc25 downregulation. Cdk5, which forms a separate complex with Pcl12 for morphogenesis, is not required for cell cycle arrest.
results.evaluation: Claims C42, C44-C45, C92-C99 are supported by genetic data (Figures 2A-E), proteomic analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), and prior citations. The LC/MS identification of Crk1 as a Pcl12 interactor is direct evidence. The genetic requirement for both proteins in cell cycle arrest is demonstrated by loss-of-function experiments. The distinction from the Pcl12-Cdk5 complex is supported by the cdk5ts experiment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

results.result: Crk1 activation for cell cycle arrest does not require phosphorylation by the MAPK cascade. Cells carrying crk1 alleles refractory to phosphorylation by Fuz7 (crk1AEF) or Kpp2 (crk1AAA) can still arrest upon fuz7DD or pcl12 expression. The authors propose Crk1 can be activated by two distinct mechanisms: as a MAPK by T-loop phosphorylation for polar growth, or as a CDK by interaction with Pcl12 for cell cycle arrest.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 are supported by genetic data showing that phosphorylation-defective crk1 alleles retain cell cycle arrest function (Figures 2F, 2C, 2—figure supplement 3). This is surprising given prior work showing these phosphorylations are required for morphogenesis. The dual activation model (C48) is a reasonable inference to explain these observations, though it remains a hypothesis requiring further mechanistic validation.

results.result: Ectopic pcl12 expression induces cell cycle arrest by excluding Cdc25 from the nucleus without decreasing Cdc25 protein levels. GFP-Cdc25 is excluded from nuclei in pcl12-expressing filaments in a Crk1-dependent manner. The Crk1-Pcl12 complex inhibits the interaction between Cdc25 and its importin Kap123, but G2 arrest alone does not.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 are supported by multiple lines of evidence: cell cycle arrest depends on Cdk1 phosphorylation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B), Cdc25 levels don't decrease (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), microscopy shows nuclear exclusion (Figures 3A-B), and co-IP shows Crk1-Pcl12 disrupts Cdc25-Kap123 interaction (Figure 3C). The control using Wee1 overexpression to induce G2 arrest without Crk1-Pcl12 is appropriate.

results.result: Kap123 is phosphorylated upon pheromone cascade activation. Kap123 shows reduced electrophoretic mobility upon fuz7DD or pcl12 expression, which is sensitive to phosphatase treatment. The mobility shift upon fuz7DD expression requires Crk1, Pcl12, and Kpp2, while pcl12-induced shift requires only Crk1. Kap123 is a β-importin of class 3/4 required for nuclear localization of Cdc25.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C58, C101 are supported by Western blot data showing mobility shifts (Figures 3D-H), phosphatase sensitivity (Figure 3E), genetic dependencies (Figures 3G-H), phylogenetic analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), and functional data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-C). The phosphatase treatment directly demonstrates phosphorylation. The genetic requirements match the cell cycle arrest requirements, supporting a causal relationship.

results.result: Phosphorylation of Kap123 at T867 is required for pheromone cascade-induced cell cycle arrest. The kap123T867A mutant shows no mobility shift upon fuz7DD or pcl12 expression, cannot undergo cell cycle arrest, cannot retain Cdc25 in the cytoplasm, and maintains interaction with Cdc25 even in the presence of Crk1-Pcl12 complex.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C63 are supported by comprehensive functional analysis of the kap123T867A mutant: Western blots (Figures 4B-C), cell cycle analysis (Figures 4D-E), microscopy (Figures 4F-G), and co-IP (Figure 4H). The identification of T867 as the critical residue was done systematically by testing multiple predicted phosphorylation sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The mutant phenotypes are consistent across all assays, strongly supporting the model.

results.result: The kap123T867A mutant cannot arrest in response to synthetic pheromone. Cells carrying this allele fail to arrest even at high pheromone concentrations, show no Kap123 mobility shift, and cannot exclude Cdc25 from the nucleus in response to pheromone.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 validate the model using physiological pheromone stimulation rather than the fuz7DD system. The data (Figures 5A-D) show consistent phenotypes: no cell cycle arrest, no Kap123 phosphorylation, and no Cdc25 nuclear exclusion. This demonstrates the mechanism operates during normal pheromone response, not just with the artificial fuz7DD system.

results.result: Strains lacking pheromone-induced cell cycle arrest (kap123T867A) are as virulent as wild-type in plant infections. These mutants can mate (positive fuzzy phenotype), but resulting filaments are multinucleated (2-4 nuclei). The kap123T867A allele does not affect b-factor-induced cell cycle arrest.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C70 are supported by plant infection data (Figure 6A), mating assays (Figure 6B), microscopy (Figures 6C-D), and b-factor arrest assays (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The unexpected finding that virulence is unaffected is explained by the authors: b-factor can resynchronize nuclei after fusion. The multinucleated filaments (2-4 nuclei) are consistent with fusion at different cell cycle stages, but b-factor prevents further divisions. This is a logical explanation supported by the data.

results.result: Cdc25 downregulation requires high pheromone signaling and cytoplasmic retention. Low pheromone (0.25 μg/ml) induces arrest without Cdc25 downregulation, while higher concentrations cause dose-dependent Cdc25 decrease. Downregulation requires cytoplasmic retention (absent in kap123T867A) and the MAPK Kpp2. Kpp2 physically interacts with Cdc25 under conditions of high MAPK signaling and cytoplasmic retention.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75, C80 are supported by dose-response experiments (Figure 7A), genetic analysis (Figures 7B-C), and co-IP (Figure 7D). The logic is sound: retention is necessary but not sufficient (pcl12 alone doesn't cause downregulation), and high MAPK activity is required (Kpp2 dependence). The physical interaction between Kpp2 and Cdc25 under specific conditions supports direct targeting. The conclusion (C80) is a reasonable inference from the data.

results.result: The N-terminal extension of Cdc25 contains MAPK phosphorylation sites required for its downregulation. U. maydis Cdc25 has an unusual 270 amino acid N-terminal extension. Deletion of this region or mutation of three putative MAPK sites (cdc25AAA) stabilizes Cdc25 upon fuz7DD expression. These mutations do not affect cell cycle arrest or cytoplasmic retention.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 are supported by sequence analysis (Figure 7E), Western blots showing stabilization (Figures 7F-G), and functional assays (Figures 7H-I). The N-terminal extension is unique to U. maydis Cdc25. Both deletion and point mutations prevent downregulation while maintaining arrest function, indicating the extension is specifically required for degradation but not for the arrest mechanism itself. This is consistent with the model.

results.result: Strains carrying the cdc25AAA allele (resistant to downregulation) are strongly defective in virulence. Compatible crosses are affected, but the solopathogenic SG200 strain is unaffected, indicating a mating-specific defect. Mutant crosses show weak fuzzy phenotype, can undergo cell fusion, but produce multinucleated filaments with >5 nuclei. The cdc25AAA allele does not affect de novo b-factor-induced arrest.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C87 are supported by plant infection data (Figure 8A), mating assays (Figure 8B), microscopy (Figures 8C-D), and b-factor arrest assays (Figure 8E). The key finding is that preventing Cdc25 downregulation causes virulence defects specifically in crosses, not in solopathogenic strains. The multinucleated filaments (>5 nuclei) contrast with kap123T867A (≤4 nuclei), suggesting the stable Cdc25 can eventually overwhelm b-factor arrest. This supports the model that Cdc25 downregulation is required for proper transition to b-dependent arrest.

results.result: The pheromone and b-factor regulatory networks use distinct mechanisms to control Cdc25. Both upregulate Wee1 by repressing hsl1, but differ in Cdc25 regulation: pheromone cascade inhibits Cdc25 nuclear import via Kap123 phosphorylation (cannot be bypassed by overexpression), while b-factor retains Cdc25 via 14-3-3 proteins and represses clb1 (can be overwhelmed by overexpression). The authors propose pheromone-dependent arrest is reversible, while b-dependent arrest is more terminal.
results.evaluation: Claims C88, C115-C126 synthesize the experimental findings into a coherent model. The mechanistic differences are well-supported by the data: overexpression experiments distinguish the two mechanisms (C39, C41, C125-C126), and the functional interpretations about reversibility (C121-C124) are logical given the biological context. The model explains why Cdc25 must be downregulated before b-factor activation: to prevent overwhelming the 14-3-3 retention system. This is supported by the cdc25AAA phenotype.

results.result: Crk1 is a member of the RD kinase family with features of both CDKs and MAPKs. It carries a TEY signature typical of MAPKs but structurally resembles Cdk2. Crk1 belongs to the Ime2 family of fungal kinases involved in sexual development. RD kinases can be activated by T-loop phosphorylation or by cyclin binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C132 provide the structural and evolutionary context for understanding Crk1's dual functionality. These are supported by citations to prior work on RD kinases (C127, C129), Crk1 structure (C130), and the Ime2 family (C131-C132). The information is consistent with the experimental observation that Crk1 can function in cell cycle arrest without MAPK-type phosphorylation when bound to Pcl12. This provides a mechanistic framework for the dual activation model.

results.result: Background on cell cycle regulation during mating in eukaryotes and fungi. Most organisms synchronize at G1 before fusion; U. maydis is exceptional in synchronizing at G2. Cell cycle-infection connections exist in other fungal pathogens. G2/M transition in U. maydis is controlled by Cdk1-Clb2 complex and Cdk1 inhibitory phosphorylation. The b-factor maintains arrest through multiple mechanisms including DDR activation and transcriptional repression.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C12, C14, C27-C28, C89-C91, C100, C102-C114 provide essential background and context. These are supported by numerous citations to prior work and represent established knowledge in the field. They set up the biological problem and provide the framework for understanding the significance of the current findings. While not novel results, they are accurately presented and appropriately cited.
